findings.statement: four independent WAL streams commit at least 2.5x one stream
findings.detail: 1 stream 2792443 records/s, 2 streams 3186933, 4 streams 4367024 (1.56x, 4-streams vs 1-stream: greater 1.564x (p=0.0122, rel_iqr 0.3%/25.5%)), 8 streams 4393668. This is P-D's 2.5x bar applied to the floor: below it the barrier serialises at the device and sharded WALs cannot deliver P-D here

findings.statement: scaling is sublinear past four streams
findings.detail: 8 streams run 1.01x of 4. Near-linear here would mean the device has more barrier concurrency than the design assumed and shard count should follow cores

findings.statement: a group commit over one file beats four independent streams
findings.detail: 4 threads under one group-committed file 3187079 records/s against 4 independent streams 4367024 (4-group vs 4-streams: less 0.730x (p=0.0122, rel_iqr 7.1%/0.3%)). One barrier amortised over four batches should cost less than four barriers if the device is the bottleneck; if independence wins, barriers are cheap in parallel and the lock is what costs

notes: five arms interleaved: 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads each owning a WAL file and committing its own framed 1,000-record batches with one fdatasync each (f39's raw-wal arm run N-wide), and 4 threads sharing one file under a group commit -- appends interleave behind a mutex and one fdatasync per round covers every thread's batch. Aggregate durable records per second. No engine work, so this is a ceiling for sharded writers and not a measurement of any
predictions registered in parwal-plan.md before the run
